title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents, 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of high‑level operator intent to device configurations is a promising avenue to reduce routine NetOps labor and speed maintenance workflows. Yet large language models (LLMs) can produce mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that have direct operational consequences (availability loss, unintended access changes, or security exposure) [1]–[3]. A widely proposed mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pattern: generate a draft configuration, run a deterministic verifier that checks mechanically expressible constraints, and—if the verifier reports localized failures—request a targeted repair from the model [2], [4].

Prior demonstrations show verifier‑grounded repair reduces mechanically checkable errors in prototype settings, but questions remain about scaling such architectures across heterogeneous vendor templates, measuring model‑call cost per avoided violation, and interpreting paired comparisons under shared_initial_candidate sampling (where the same initial model output is reused across conditions). To address these gaps we preregistered study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 and executed a paired, provenance‑traced Mininet emulation experiment that exercises three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns. Our preregistered primary estimand compares the probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable violations under guarded (GVR) versus baseline (single‑shot LLM) generation using an exact McNemar two‑sided test.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps and AIOps research while highlighting evaluation gaps: benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. Prototype NetOps studies and adjacent domain work show LLMs can draft device configurations or configuration‑like artifacts but often introduce syntax/topology or policy errors; closed‑loop verifier‑guided repair recurs as an empirically supported mitigation pattern in code and domain‑specific program generation [2], [3]. Other verified/empirical demonstrations emphasize that verifier utility depends on (a) having mechanizable domain rules, (b) producing localized, actionable feedback, and (c) measuring cost tradeoffs (additional model calls per avoided error) [7], [8].

Our experiment builds on these prior contributions by (i) applying a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory design across heterogeneous synthetic vendor templates in an emulator, (ii) enforcing and documenting shared_initial_candidate semantics so differences derive only from validator/repair actions, and (iii) recording full provider and verifier accounting to quantify repair cost in concrete hosted‑LLM call counts. We do not claim broader production readiness; rather we position this work as an artifact‑grounded proof‑of‑concept evaluation of a verifier‑grounded pipeline under tightly specified scope.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 prior to any model calls. The primary estimand (confirmatory) is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, evaluated with an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary per‑intent success indicators (success = no operationally detectable policy violations after the applicable pipeline completes). The preregistration SHA‑256 is 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50.

Sampling, strata, and shared_initial_candidate semantics: The experiment used N = 200 deterministically selected unique operator intents stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) per the frozen task_index_profile. Episodes were paired: for each intent exactly one initial generation was sampled and the same generated candidate was reused by both baseline and guarded episodes (registered and executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics). Consequently, for a given intent the baseline outcome is the validator score on that shared initial candidate; the guarded outcome is the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. Because of shared_initial_candidate semantics, any paired outcome difference can arise only from deterministic validator/repair actions (not from independent first‑pass sampling or different prompt templates). The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; readers should interpret results accordingly.

Model, sampling notes, and budget: The declared model in the archived execution manifest is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses) and the archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset. We state explicitly that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The preregistered budget: planned_episode_count = 400, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_model_calls = 400.

Deterministic validator and repair policy: The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements syntactic parsing, required‑command sequencing checks, reachability/topology verification against the emulated network state, and encoded ACL/policy checks derived from the task payload constraints. The guarded pipeline permitted up to one verifier‑triggered repair call per intent; repairs were requested only when the validator reported violations and the repair prompt used the validator's localized failure diagnostics to guide the model. Validator verdicts are boolean per the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule (success if no detected violations).

Scoring, primary analysis, and exploratory estimators: The preregistered primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired success indicators (α = 0.05). Exploratory analyses (declared a priori in the preregistration) include a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics: mean extra hosted model calls per intent and mean extra calls per avoided violation. Missingness and exclusions follow the preregistered rules; in execution no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed.

Deterministic accounting and provider audit: Execution manifest audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 204. Stage accounting decomposes these calls as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls; cache_hit_count = 0 and cache_miss_count = 204. The manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts verify complete episode accounting (planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200). We report these audited counts verbatim in Results to allow independent reconciliation with archived artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution and paired outcomes: The run completed as preregistered (completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; do not reject at α = 0.05). The archived paired bootstrap (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]; this bootstrap CI was preregistered as exploratory and supplemental to the confirmatory McNemar test. We emphasize the study's formal confirmatory inference is the McNemar result and treat the bootstrap interval as descriptive context for effect magnitude.

Repair and cost accounting: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents (repair_calls = 4). Total hosted model calls recorded = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repairs). From these audited counts we compute mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02; mean extra calls per intent due to guarded repairs = 0.02; mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0 (four repairs correspond to four baseline failures corrected under guarded pipeline). The execution_manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts contain the provider_call audit enabling independent verification of these arithmetic derivations.

Representative artifacts and validator traces: Representative execution/responses and execution/scoring entries included in the archived bundle show that for each example the same shared initial candidate text file was used by both conditions and that validator_trace.validation_after records whether repairs were applied and the final validator verdict. These artifacts substantiate the contingency counts and the repair accounting reported above.

Statistical diagnostics and sparse‑discordance caution: Discordant pair count (n10 + n01 = 4) is small. In sparse‑discordance regimes exact conditional tests (McNemar) and resampling‑based intervals can give differing signals (as here). We therefore emphasize the preregistered McNemar test as the formal confirmatory inference and present the bootstrap CI for magnitude interpretation only, noting potential instability of resampling estimates when discordant counts are small.

Deviations, missingness, and execution integrity: No preregistered deviations were recorded; missingness summary reports complete_pairs = 200. The deterministic_reconciliation checks passed and provider_call_audit fields are internally consistent (hosted_model_call_event_count = 204; no failed model calls). All reported numerical values are drawn verbatim from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/*.csv and execution/* manifests).
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs exploratory interpretation: The preregistered exact McNemar test is the study's formal confirmatory analysis and did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). The observed point estimate (0.02) and the exploratory bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] provide complementary context about effect magnitude but do not overturn the preregistered confirmatory conclusion. Because the shared_initial_candidate design reuses the same draft across conditions, the observed guarded improvements derive exclusively from deterministic validator/repair activity rather than differences in first‑pass sampling or prompt templates.

Operational interpretation and bounded implications: Within the constrained Mininet emulation, synthetic vendor templates, and the encoded validator rule set, a small repair budget (4 repairs over 200 intents) removed the mechanically detectable baseline violations. The low absolute baseline failure prevalence (2%) implies that modest repair activity sufficed in this workload. These results suggest that when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and provides actionable feedback, bounded repair budgets can materially reduce mechanically checkable faults in template‑driven emulated settings. We do not claim that this finding generalizes to production hardware, different prompt families, other models, or to semantic errors outside the validator's rule coverage.

Threats to validity: Construct validity—the deterministic validator covers syntactic, topology, and encoded ACL/policy checks, but cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations not expressible in its rule set. Internal validity—the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed; this design prevents attributing observed gains to prompt engineering or independent re‑sampling. Conclusion validity—low discordant counts limit power to detect small absolute effects; bootstrap intervals may be unstable in such regimes. External validity—the experiment used a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic templates, and Mininet emulation; results do not imply production‑grade safety or multi‑model generality.

Recommendations and follow‑ups that remain consistent with archived evidence: (1) Extend deterministic validator coverage to formalize additional semantic/policy ontologies and quantify residual false negatives. (2) Repeat paired designs with independent multi‑sample initial generations to measure effects attributable to constrained prompting or prompt templates (this was not executed here). (3) Evaluate multiple hosted models and model versions to assess robustness to provider nondeterminism. (4) Maintain provenance tracing for all provider calls and validator traces to support reproducibility and independent audit. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifact evidence and listed limitations.
sections.conclusion:
We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to measure whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent‑to‑configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a deterministic verifier can express and check relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator. Future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
